extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in misinformation and media in India
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of fake news in India
extracted.subtask_description: A country-level encyclopedic survey of fake news in India: definitions and typologies, notable incidents and themes, modes of distribution, impacts, detection challenges, and countermeasures by platforms, media and government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is defined as stories purporting to be news that are intentionally and verifiably false and has the capacity to misinform and mislead readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the working definition for the article; distinguishes deliberately false news from other forms of inaccurate reporting. Examples and effects (e.g., mob violence) are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic typology (axes for classifying fake news)
rubrics_metrics.description: In academic typology, fake news is classified into several forms along the axes of degree of facticity, motivation of deception and form of presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes satire and parody (may have basis in facts but mislead when decontextualised), fabrications and manipulation created to deceive, and covert advertising and political propaganda aimed to influence public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: UNESCO distinction: disinformation vs misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: UNESCO distinguishes two forms: one deliberately created with the intention of targeting and causing harm to a social group, organisation, person or country (disinformation), and the other being simple misinformation that wasn't created for the purpose of causing harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is used to separate intent-driven campaigns from accidental or poorly-sourced falsehoods; relevant for legal, ethical and remedial responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source / origin of fake news (creators)
rubrics_metrics.description: In India, fake news is predominantly disseminated by homegrown political disinformation campaigns; reporting cites an ecosystem close to the ruling BJP and supporters creating and highlighting disinformation that serves political interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying origin/networks (political cells, companies, organised influence networks) is central to attributing campaigns; article gives examples (BJP IT cell, Srivastava Group) and investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common themes and targets of fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring themes include public health (COVID‑19), protests and legislation (e.g., CAA), elections, anti‑Pakistan propaganda, Kashmir-related misinformation, communal/ethnic tensions (e.g., anti‑Hindu/Bangladesh stories), and international conflicts (e.g., Israel–Palestine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article documents numerous examples showing how particular events/topics are repeatedly exploited; useful for prioritising monitoring and fact‑checking efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of distribution / channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is fostered and spread through word of mouth, traditional media and digital forms such as edited videos, websites, blogs, memes, unverified advertisements and social media‑propagated rumours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific platforms called out include WhatsApp, Facebook/Meta and Twitter/X; propagation often involves viral forwards, channels, and reuse by mainstream outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact dimensions (socio‑political and institutional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news can result in mob violence and localized or large-scale riots, target minorities, instigate engineered mass violence, and produce institutional responses such as internet shutdowns and constraints on press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited incidents (e.g., 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, WhatsApp‑linked killings) illustrate direct harms; institutional impacts include government monitoring, policy changes, and UN/rights‑based concerns about restrictions on expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of fake news websites and networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake websites often copy syndicated content from real news sites to appear legitimate, plant opinion pieces and stories from linked NGO members, falsely attribute articles, invent journalists, use plagiarised text, create fake personas and organisations, impersonate agencies and cybersquat domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article gives examples (EU Chronicle, Manchester Times style domains, Srivastava Group) and shows how these indicators can be used to detect and flag inauthentic sites and networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mainstream media amplification risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream Indian news outlets sometimes reuse and republish material from fake websites, amplifying disinformation to millions; the article documents instances where mainstream media spread misinformation (including during conflicts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the need for newsroom verification and editorial standards to prevent circular reporting and amplification of manufactured content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges in detection and vetting (multilingual and resource constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: India's linguistic diversity (22 scheduled languages) and limited vetting resources mean platforms have difficulty vetting content in many languages (example: Facebook had resources to vet ~10 languages as of May 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits multinational platforms' effectiveness and creates gaps exploited by disinformation actors; suggests prioritising localized capacity and language coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact‑checking and verification infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact‑checking in India includes dedicated websites (BOOM, Alt News, Factly, SMHoaxSlayer), media house fact‑check teams (India Today Group, TOI Factcheck, The Quint's WebQoof), and partnerships (IFCN‑certified organisations partnering with Facebook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of tools and initiatives (Google's 'About This Result') and training programs (Google training journalists) are cited as verification resources and capacity‑building measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation and technical interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms have implemented measures such as limiting the number of forwards (WhatsApp), adding 'forwarded' tags, introducing tip‑lines, suspending accounts, deleting accounts (Twitter), and partnering with fact‑checkers (Facebook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes concrete platform actions and their evolution, and references outcomes like account removals and feature rollouts; these techniques are presented as partial mitigations with varying effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental and legal countermeasures and their tensions with free expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses include arrests for spreading false information, formation of monitoring centres (e.g., Tamil Nadu Social Media Monitoring Centre), government fact‑checking modules (FACT: Find, Assess, Create and Target), Press Information Bureau units, and policies like J&K's Media Policy (de‑empaneling and legal proceedings for 'fake news').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article records both implementation and criticism: UN rapporteurs and press bodies warn that vague prohibitions on 'false news' can threaten freedom of expression and independent journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grassroots education and public‑awareness measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Local initiatives include fake news classes in government schools, public‑education campaigns, and large training programs for journalists (e.g., Google's program to train 8,000 journalists in Indian languages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as preventative measures to improve digital/media literacy; article cites calls for expanded public education to raise awareness of fake news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed technical/policy suggestions and controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals recorded in the article include ideas like linking Aadhaar to social media accounts to check fake news and government efforts to publicize information (e.g., Supreme Court urging publicity about CAA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proposals are controversial and cited alongside critiques about privacy, feasibility and risks to civil liberties; article provides context and responses from stakeholders.
